headline: Tech Rebound and Pricey Oil Nudge Rates Higher
tileReason: The daily 30-year average rose to about 7.43% Monday as tech stocks bounced back and oil stayed near $110, pulling money out of safe-haven bonds.
takeaway: Rates gave back a bit more of last week's drop on Monday. The daily 30-year average rose 0.06% to 7.43% as tech stocks had their best day in weeks and investors moved money out of the safety of bonds. Oil also stayed expensive, near $110 a barrel for Brent, after new attacks on Saudi energy sites and fresh tension around the Strait of Hormuz. This morning the 10-year Treasury yield has eased slightly to about 5.11%, and September housing starts came in weak, so lenders are likely to price close to Monday, perhaps a touch better. Traders still see only about a 1-in-6 chance of a Fed hike on October 28, but nearly all expect one in December. Over the next month, the odds are close to even, with hot inflation and oil keeping higher rates very much in play.

fedOdds.title: Odds of a Fed hike on Oct 28
fedOdds.source: CME FedWatch via Benzinga (Oct 20, 6:13 AM ET), Southeast AgNET (Oct 20) and Trading Economics (Oct 20)
fedOdds.note: CME FedWatch shows about 83% to 85% odds of no change, so roughly a 15% to 17% chance of a hike. Reports of last Wednesday's post-CPI peak range from 44% to 54%. Odds of a December hike are put near 90% (CNBC via CappNotes, Southeast AgNET); Trading Economics cites reports ranging from about 75% to 94%.

drivers.title: Tech stocks bounce, pulling money out of bonds
drivers.text: Last week, worries about AI spending sent investors fleeing stocks for the safety of Treasury bonds, which pushed yields and mortgage rates down. On Monday, chip and tech stocks had their best day in weeks, and some of that money flowed back out of bonds. When bond prices fall, their yields rise. The 10-year Treasury yield rose about 0.05% to near 5.14%, and the daily 30-year average climbed 0.06% to 7.43%.

drivers.title: Oil stays near $110 on Middle East attacks
drivers.text: New Houthi attacks on Saudi energy sites and tighter Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz kept Brent crude near $110 a barrel, close to a five-month high. This morning Iran also threatened undersea data cables in the Strait. Expensive energy feeds inflation, and bond investors demand higher yields when they expect inflation to stay high, which keeps upward pressure on mortgage rates. The weekend's easing of sanctions on Russian energy has only partly offset this.

drivers.title: December Fed hike still widely expected
drivers.text: After hot September inflation reports, markets see only about a 15% to 17% chance of a hike on October 28, but around 90% odds of one in December. A White House economic adviser said this week that inflation now needs some work. Expected Fed hikes push up shorter-term yields, and that keeps a floor under longer-term rates like mortgages.

drivers.title: Housing starts slump in September
drivers.text: Builders started homes at about a 1.22 million annual pace in September, down roughly 5% to 6% from August, and single-family permits also fell. Weak housing and a home-builder confidence reading at its lowest since 2012 point to a slowing economy, which tends to help bonds a little and nudge rates down. The 10-year yield eased to about 5.11% this morning.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates are still unusually far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The daily 30-year average is running about 2.3% above the 10-year Treasury yield, compared with a more typical 2.0%. That extra cushion means mortgage rates have room to improve if markets calm down, even without a big drop in Treasury yields.

outlook.basis: It's close to a coin flip, with a slight lean toward steady. The gap between mortgage rates and the 10-year Treasury is still wider than usual (about 2.3% vs. a typical 2.0%), so rates can improve if markets calm down, and housing data is weakening. Against that, oil is back near $110, inflation keeps running hot, a December Fed hike is widely expected, and last week's bond rally is fading as tech stocks recover. The October 28 Fed decision, the October 29 inflation (PCE) data, the November 6 jobs report and the November 10 CPI report are the big swing events.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average is about 7.43%, still a bit below the 7.5% range from early October. With hot inflation and a Fed meeting on October 28, it's worth asking your lender how a lock, a float-down option, or a short wait would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates in the mid-7% range still stretch buyers' budgets, and new construction is slowing. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to buy down their rate, can help your home stand out.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Rates ticked up to about 7.43% Monday as tech stocks bounced and oil stayed high, but they're still a little below where they were two weeks ago.
